APP STORE & GOOGLE PLAY ASSET CHECKER · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Catch the icon the store is about to reject — before you upload

Drop your store-listing images in and check them against the store's requirements: an app icon that declares transparency (the classic "can't contain an alpha channel" rejection, which arrives at upload time, after the build), an icon or feature graphic at the wrong pixel size, a HEIC or WebP renamed to .png, and a screenshot set whose members disagree about their own dimensions.

Nothing is uploaded. Your files are read in this browser — only each file's first few dozen header bytes are examined, no pixels are decoded, and no filename, size or result is transmitted or stored anywhere.

1. Check your listing images

Drop your screenshots and icon here

or

Files named like AppIcon.png, ic_launcher-playstore.png or feature-graphic.png are recognised as an icon or feature graphic; everything else is treated as a screenshot.

2. Files read

FileTreated asFormatSize

Findings

Prefer a CLI, or want this as a release gate?

The CLI runs the same checks over a directory of assets and exits non-zero when something would block the upload — so a wrong-size screenshot fails the build instead of the release:

node check.mjs ./fastlane/screenshots/en-US
node check.mjs --store play ./play/listing
node check.mjs ./screenshots --json
node check.mjs ./screenshots --strict   # notices fail too

Get check.mjs, engine.mjs, image.mjs and spec.mjs from the repo — plain Node 18+, nothing to install. It opens no sockets and writes nothing: it reads the header bytes of the files you name and prints a report. Exit code 1 when a danger-severity finding is produced, 2 when the arguments or paths could not be used.

What's checked

CheckWhat it flagsSeverity
Icon transparencyAn App Store icon with an alpha channel or a tRNS chunkDanger
Icon dimensionsAn icon that is not exactly the size the store requiresDanger
File formatA file whose real bytes are HEIC, WebP, GIF or similar — whatever it is namedDanger
Set consistencyScreenshots in one set that disagree about their pixel dimensionsDanger
Screenshot countMore screenshots than the store accepts per setDanger
Play boundsA side outside 320–3840px, or an aspect ratio past 2:1Danger
Feature graphicA Play feature graphic that is not exactly 1024×500, or is transparentDanger
Mixed orientationPortrait and landscape images in the same setNotice
Unrecognised sizeA screenshot matching no display class in this tool's tableNotice
Icon encodingAn interlaced PNG, or one deeper than 8 bits per channelNotice

More: why store uploads get rejected, and the four mistakes that cause most of it. See also: how this differs from checking the spec sheet by hand.

Common questions

Why does App Store Connect reject an app icon for transparency?

Apple requires the App Store icon to be fully opaque, and the check happens at upload time — after the build and the archive, at the most expensive point in a release to discover it. A PNG declares transparency in two ways: its IHDR colour type can include an alpha channel (types 4 and 6), or a tRNS chunk can make specific colours transparent in an image that has no alpha channel at all. Both count. The fix is to flatten the icon onto an opaque background and re-export; exporting as JPEG also works, since JPEG has no alpha channel. Do not draw the rounded corners yourself — the store masks them for you, and a pre-masked icon is what usually leaves transparent corners behind.

Why does this read the file's bytes instead of its extension?

Because the extension is usually the thing that lied. Renaming a HEIC screenshot from an iPhone, or a WebP from an Android device, to .png does not convert it — the bytes stay HEIC or WebP, and the store reads the bytes. A checker that trusts the filename passes exactly the file that is about to be rejected. This tool identifies each file from its magic bytes, so a misnamed file is reported as what it actually is.

What does it mean that a screenshot set is inconsistent?

A set of screenshots uploaded for one display class has to agree with itself about its pixel dimensions. The ordinary way a set breaks is that some of it was regenerated on a newer simulator or a different device and the rest was kept — the files look fine individually and the mismatch is invisible in a file listing. This check needs no specification at all: it compares the files with each other, so it cannot go out of date when a store changes its size tables.

Are the size tables in this tool authoritative?

No, and it is built to say so. The checks split in two. Structural checks — is this really a PNG, does this icon declare transparency, do these screenshots agree with each other — are answered from the files themselves and cannot go stale. Table checks compare against a transcription of each store's published sizes, and Apple and Google add and retire device classes, so a size this tool does not recognise is reported as a notice that names the table as the thing that might be wrong, never as a failure. Each store's own current documentation is authoritative.

Is anything uploaded when I drop images on this page?

No. The files are read in your browser with the File API and only the first few dozen header bytes of each are examined — no pixels are decoded, no image is transmitted, and no filename, dimension or result is recorded anywhere. Your unreleased app's artwork stays on your machine. The page keeps only an anonymous local count of how many times the check button was pressed, which you can switch off below.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, business, or app-review advice, and it does not replace reading each store's own current documentation. It reports whether the image files you provided satisfy specific, mechanically checkable rules — nothing more. It is not a guarantee that a submission will be accepted, and passing every check here does not mean an app will pass review. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Not affiliated with Apple or Google. "App Store", "App Store Connect", "Google Play" and "Google Play Console" are the trademarks of their respective owners, used here only to say which store's published requirements a check refers to. The size tables in this tool were last reviewed on 2026-09-11 and may be out of date; each store's own documentation is authoritative.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get check.mjs and run it yourself.

Every file you drop here is read in your browser and is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (check_run, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Also worth a pass before you ship: App Listing Metadata Check lints your listing text and keyword field, and iOS Privacy Manifest Check catches a missing required-reason API declaration before App Review does. Social Preview Check checks the card your links produce when shared. PWA Installability Check checks a web app manifest's own install requirements.

Free and open source. If this caught a rejected icon before your release did, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-manual-checking.html.text:
← App Store Screenshot & Icon Checker

Checking store assets by hand vs. automatically

Most people check store assets by opening the spec page in one window and the asset folder in another. That genuinely works for the thing it is good at — dimensions — and misses four things it structurally cannot see. This page is about which is which, including where the manual approach is the better one.

What each approach actually sees

ProblemSpec sheet + file browserThis tool
Wrong pixel dimensionsYes — this is what it is good atYes
Icon declares an alpha channelNo — not shown in Get Info or PropertiesYes, from the PNG colour type
Icon transparent via a tRNS chunkNoYes
HEIC or WebP renamed to .pngNo — the name is what it reportsYes, from magic bytes
Screenshot set disagreeing with itselfIn principle, by comparing every file by eye, every releaseYes, automatically
Interlaced or 16-bit PNGNoYes
Whether the artwork is any goodYes — you are looking at itNo. It never decodes a pixel
Whether a screenshot honestly shows the appYesNo

The last two rows are the honest limit of any mechanical checker, and they are not small. Nothing here judges whether your screenshots are worth looking at or whether they represent the app fairly — which is what app review will actually be assessing.

Common questions

Can't I just check the dimensions in Finder or Explorer?

You can, and for dimensions alone it works. What a file browser will not tell you is whether a PNG declares an alpha channel — macOS Get Info and Windows Properties both show the pixel size and the file size, neither shows the colour type — and that is the property behind the most common upload rejection. It also will not tell you that a file named .png is really a HEIC, because it reports what the name implies. And comparing ten files' dimensions against each other by eye, on every release, is exactly the kind of task a person does correctly nine times and then does not.

Why not open the icon in an image editor and look at it?

Because an alpha channel is invisible when every pixel in it is opaque. An icon can look completely solid against the editor's white canvas, export with a full alpha channel, and be rejected — the store reads the declaration in the file header, not the appearance of the pixels. The only way to see it by eye is to know where your editor hides the channel list, and to remember to look there during every release.

Is a paid asset-preparation service better than this?

For generating assets, very possibly — resizing one screenshot into every display class, adding device frames and captions, and uploading the result is real work that dedicated tools do well, and this tool does none of it. This is a checker, not a generator. It reads assets you already have and tells you what would be refused. The two are complementary: a generator's output is exactly the kind of thing worth checking, since a bug in a resize pipeline produces a whole set of consistently wrong files.

Why would I want this in CI rather than just on a web page?

Because the failure it prevents is a release-day failure, and release day is the worst time to be reading a spec sheet. A checked-in screenshot set drifts the same way any other checked-in artefact does — someone regenerates part of it, someone adds a locale, someone's export preset changes. Running the CLI on every pull request that touches the asset directory turns that drift into a failed build, at the point where it costs a minute instead of a release cycle.

No warranty. This page and the tool it describes are provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, business, or app-review advice, and it does not replace reading each store's own current documentation. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying any output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

why-store-uploads-get-rejected.html.text:
← App Store Screenshot & Icon Checker

Why store uploads get rejected for images

Four problems account for most of it. None of them is a design judgement — every one is a mechanical property of the file, which is why every one can be caught before you upload rather than after. You can check your own assets against all four with the browser tool or the CLI.

1. The app icon declares transparency

This is the expensive one, because of when it fires. The icon is validated at upload time — after the build, after the archive, often after a CI pipeline that took twenty minutes — and the message you get back is about an alpha channel rather than about anything you can see on screen.

What is an alpha channel, and why does an icon have one by accident?

An alpha channel is a fourth value stored alongside red, green and blue that says how opaque each pixel is. Most design tools export PNG with one whether or not any pixel is actually transparent — the channel is a property of the file format, not of the artwork. So an icon that looks completely solid can still declare transparency, and the store checks the declaration. Exporting from a template with rounded corners is the other common source: the corners really are transparent, because the designer masked them, and the store was going to mask them anyway.

There is a second route that catches people who have already learned the first. A PNG with no alpha channel at all can still be transparent, via a tRNS chunk that nominates particular colours as see-through. Palette PNGs — the kind an "optimise for web" export step produces — use this routinely. A checker that only looks at the colour type misses it.

The fix: flatten the icon onto an opaque background and re-export. Exporting as JPEG also removes it, since JPEG has no alpha channel in any baseline form. Do not draw the rounded corners yourself; submit a full square and let the store mask it.

2. The screenshot set disagrees with itself

Why does a screenshot set need to be internally consistent?

Each screenshot set belongs to one display class, and every image in it is shown at the same size in the same carousel. Mixed sizes in one set is not a stylistic problem, it is a set that cannot be uploaded. It happens when part of a set is regenerated — a new simulator, a redesigned screen, one screenshot replaced after a bug fix — and the rest is left alone. Nothing about the individual files looks wrong, which is why it survives a visual check and fails at upload.

This is the check worth having most, and the one a specification cannot help you with: it is answered by comparing the files with each other. It is also the check that stays correct forever, because there is no published table involved that could go out of date.

3. The file is not the format its name claims

Why doesn't renaming a HEIC to .png work?

A file's format is determined by its contents, not its name. HEIC files begin with an ISO base media ftyp box; PNG files begin with an eight-byte signature. Renaming changes neither. Every tool that actually reads the file — including the store's upload validator — sees HEIC. The fix is to re-export or convert, which on macOS can be done in Preview with File → Export and a format of PNG.

Screenshots taken on a physical iPhone and pulled through Photos are the usual source on the Apple side; a WebP saved from a browser is the usual one on the Android side. Both are easy to rename and impossible to fix by renaming.

4. A size is simply wrong

The fixed sizes are the ones worth being certain about: a 1024×1024 App Store icon, a 512×512 Play icon, a 1024×500 Play feature graphic. Those have been stable for the life of both stores and a mismatch is unambiguous.

Screenshot sizes are different, and it is worth being clear about why. Apple publishes a list of display classes and adds to it with each hardware generation; Google publishes bounds (a minimum and maximum side length, and a maximum aspect ratio) rather than a list. A tool that hard-codes Apple's list will eventually flag a perfectly good screenshot from a device it has not heard of. That is why this tool reports an unrecognised size as a notice that names its own table as the suspect, and reserves hard failures for the things it can be certain about.

What this does not cover

Does passing these checks mean my app will be approved?

No. These are upload-time asset validations: they decide whether the listing images can be attached at all. App review is a separate, later, human process that judges the app itself — its functionality, its privacy declarations, its content, and whether the screenshots honestly represent what the app does. Passing every check in this tool only means the images are well-formed enough to be uploaded.
